me-home-heating-costs-neada-2026-10-01.excerpt: A new regional estimate puts the average Maine household's heating-oil cost 77% above last winter, as state data show prices above $6 a gallon and assistance applications open.
me-home-heating-costs-neada-2026-10-01.text: maine oil-heating bills projected to approach $3,000 this winter a new regional estimate puts the average maine household's heating-oil cost 77% above last winter, as state data show prices above $6 a gallon and assistance applications open. maine households that heat with oil are facing a sharply more expensive winter, with the average cost projected to reach $2,939, according to a september 29 report by wmtw news 8 citing the national energy assistance directors association. the estimate is for the 2026-27 heating season and does not represent a guaranteed bill for every household. the projected figure is 77% higher than the $1,664 comparison figure reported for last winter. wmtw said that increase is tied with vermont for the largest projected rise among states in the northeast. the comparison is especially significant in maine, where heating oil remains a major household fuel and where many homes begin the heating season with little room for a large price shock. the estimate arrived as maine's own fuel survey showed oil prices at $6.02 per gallon. the maine department of energy resources reported that statewide average on september 21, with surveyed prices ranging from $5.00 to $6.45. the department cautions that the figures are cash prices from delivered-fuel retailers, not pre-buy or discounted contracts, and that local prices can vary considerably. its current price page is https://www.maine.gov/energy/heating-fuel-prices. a seasonal average is not the same as a forecast for an individual home. actual spending will depend on the amount of oil a household uses, the size and efficiency of the building, the length and severity of the cold season, and the price charged by the local supplier. the projection also describes heating-oil users; households using propane, natural gas, wood or electricity will face different costs. maine's energy office says its comparison dashboard is intended to show relative heating costs and does not include the cost of installing a new heating system. the price pressure matters beyond the monthly fuel bill. a household that spends more to heat its home has less money available for rent, food, transportation and medical expenses. it can also make the timing of a delivery important: a family that delays an order while waiting for a lower price may still need fuel before the weather turns colder. maine's department of energy resources publishes a winter-heating guide and updates its delivered-fuel survey during the heating season, giving consumers a way to compare the statewide benchmark with local offers. state assistance is available for eligible households, but it is income- and household-size based. mainehousing says its home energy assistance program helps qualified homeowners and renters with heating costs, fuel deliveries, energy-related repairs and some utility payments. applications for the 2026-27 heap season opened august 3 and continue until funds are exhausted or may 29, 2027. details and the application are available at https://www.mainehousing.org/programs-services/energy/energydetails/liheap. mainehousing also says crisis assistance for households with extremely low fuel supplies will open november 1. that program requires a heap application first and is administered through local community action agencies. the agency encourages residents to apply early, because benefits depend on eligibility and available funds. for readers trying to plan, the immediate next steps are to check the current local price, review the state's assistance rules and avoid treating the $2,939 projection as a promise that every home will spend the same amount. maine maine maine me augusta maine maine heating oil home heating energy costs mainehousing heap affordability

me-maine-roads-to-quality-contract-2026-.excerpt: DHHS conditionally selected New York-based Shine Early Learning for two contracts worth an estimated $10 million, a decision that could end the University of Southern Maine's decades-long role supporting child-care providers.
me-maine-roads-to-quality-contract-2026-.text: maine child-development contracts put long-running usm program at risk dhhs conditionally selected new york-based shine early learning for two contracts worth an estimated $10 million, a decision that could end the university of southern maine's decades-long role supporting child-care providers. maine has conditionally selected an out-of-state company to take over two child-development support contracts, putting the future of maine roads to quality at the university of southern maine in doubt and raising questions about how the state will deliver training and technical help to early-childhood providers. the department of health and human services offered the contracts to shine early learning, a new york-based company whose work includes services for child-care centers, home-based providers and public schools in more than 30 states. the two awards are estimated at about $10 million over two years, according to [centralmaine.com and the portland press herald](https://www.centralmaine.com/2026/10/01/maine-dhhs-awards-child-development-grant-to-out-of-state-private-equity-backed-firm/). dhhs spokesperson lindsay hammes told the newspapers that the awards remain conditional and that the final value will be public after the contracts are completed; no contracts had been ratified when the report was published. one contract covers coaching, credentialing and training for early-childhood educators and care providers. the other would provide a dhhs-approved training plan intended to improve the quality of child-care services and the educators who provide them. those functions have been housed under one contract for much of the program's history, according to samantha warren, a university of maine system spokesperson quoted by centralmaine.com. maine roads to quality was created in 1999 through the catherine cutler institute at usm. the program provides professional development and assistance to more than 10,000 maine child-care providers each year, the newspaper reported. a [university of maine program description](https://ccids.umaine.edu/research-projects/mrtq-pdn/) says the broader professional-development network also supports a child-care database, specialized training, inclusion consultation and a warm line for providers seeking advice. the university page identifies the network's funding as a maine dhhs office of child and family services block grant. that infrastructure is tied to how maine evaluates and supports child-care quality. the [maine dhhs description of rising stars for me](https://www11.maine.gov/dhhs/ocfs/support-for-families/child-care/qris) says the quality-rating system is funded by the federal child care and development fund and administered by the department's office of child and family services. the maine department of education says public-preschool staff must join the maine roads to quality registry and describes the network as providing free or low-cost training in person, online and in hybrid formats. a change in the operator therefore affects more than a single university program; it touches a statewide system that providers use for professional development and quality-rating work. the competing proposals received sharply different scores. shine's bid earned 97 out of 100 for the coaching contract and a perfect score for the training-plan contract, while maine roads received about 73 points on each proposal, centralmaine.com reported. the state said the scores followed the process in its requests for proposals but did not explain the difference in detail. the newspaper also reported that shine's proposals were about $2 million lower across the two contracts, though dhhs has not published the final contract values because the awards are not complete. shine's applications propose using artificial intelligence in several parts of the work, including a family-navigation assistant, an employee-vetting tool and an agent to manage a provider registry, according to the report. those are plans in the company's applications, not evidence that the tools have been deployed in maine or that they will replace particular services. the contracts also require shine to employ at least 10 people in maine, a staffing condition that leaves open how much of the current locally based support model would continue. maine roads employs more than 30 people, and the university of maine system said layoffs are expected if the dhhs contracts are not renewed. the system told centralmaine.com that it plans to continue providing services through the end of the current contract and support employees who may be affected. it also plans to appeal the decision. for providers, the immediate issue is continuity: the state has announced a conditional selection, but it has not yet published a completed agreement or a transition schedule that explains when shine would assume the work. the next checkpoint is the contract process itself. dhhs will have to finalize the awards, disclose the completed values and set the terms for staffing, training, data systems and provider support. until that happens, the selection signals a possible change in who administers a core piece of maine's early-childhood infrastructure, but it does not by itself close maine roads to quality or establish exactly how services will look under the proposed new operator. maine maine maine me portland maine maine child care early childhood education maine dhhs university of southern maine state contracts artificial intelligence

me-menhaden-season-closes-quota-2026-10-.excerpt: The state says harvesters have landed 98.7% of Maine's available menhaden quota, extending a season shaped by a 20% coastwide cut and transfers from other states.
me-menhaden-season-closes-quota-2026-10-.text: maine menhaden fishery set to close sunday as quota nears completion the state says harvesters have landed 98.7% of maine's available menhaden quota, extending a season shaped by a 20% coastwide cut and transfers from other states. maine's commercial atlantic menhaden season is scheduled to close sunday night after state regulators said harvesters had landed 98.7% of the available quota, a deadline that will affect the bait supply used by lobster and other coastal fisheries. the maine department of marine resources said in a september 28 notice that it expected the remaining quota to be taken after additional fishing on september 28 and october 1. the department set the closure for 11:59 p.m. sunday, october 4, and told harvesters to complete their final reports. the notice applies to all menhaden harvesters, even though the department's general 2026 season framework had listed may 1 through november 30 as the season window. the current closure notice is at https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/medmr/bulletins/42cdf35. the compressed ending reflects a difficult quota year. the atlantic states marine fisheries commission reduced the coastwide total allowable catch for 2026 to 186,840 metric tons, a 20% decrease from the prior level. maine's department of marine resources said the reduction was intended to lower fishing mortality while protecting predators such as striped bass. maine's preliminary state quota was set at 19,599,137 pounds, with another 4,119,117 pounds reserved for its episodic event set-aside program. the agency's management page is https://www.maine.gov/dmr/fisheries/commercial/fisheries-by-species/menhaden-atlantic/menhaden-management. maine officials also said transfers from partner states helped keep the directed fishery open into october. the department said it received twice as much transferred quota as in the previous effort, despite the coastwide reduction. that choice allowed fishermen to keep using purse seines rather than shifting in mid-september to the small-scale provision, which carries different gear and quota rules. the state described the decision as a way to preserve additional harvest opportunity while staying within the available allocation. the stakes extend beyond the boats that catch menhaden. the atlantic states marine fisheries commission describes menhaden as a forage species for striped bass, bluefish and weakfish, and says commercial bait landings are used mostly in lobster, crab and hook-and-line fisheries. the commission's species overview says the 2026 quota has a zero-percent modeled chance of overfishing under its current assessment, while the stock is not classified as overfished. those findings do not remove the economic effect of a smaller quota on bait users. seafoodsource reported that maine lobster groups viewed the 20% cut as less severe than proposals for reductions of more than 50%, while still warning that any cut could affect the small-boat fleet: https://www.seafoodsource.com/news/supply-trade/asmfc-cuts-atlantic-menhaden-quota-by-20-percent-in-2026. the next debate is already underway. the commission has scheduled a virtual public hearing for 6 p.m. thursday, october 1, on draft addendum ii to the interstate menhaden plan. the proposal considers reducing the chesapeake bay reduction-fishery cap by as much as 50% and distributing that cap more evenly over the fishing season. the commission says the options are intended to address concentrated fishing effort and possible ecological effects in the bay. public comments are due by 11:59 p.m. october 9. hearing and comment details are available at https://asmfc.org/events/general-public-hearing-on-atlantic-menhaden-draft-addendum-ii/. for maine harvesters, the immediate question is operational: how much quota remains after the final scheduled fishing day and how will the closure affect bait inventories heading into the fall lobster season. the department of marine resources has not announced an extension beyond october 4 in its current notice. longer-term decisions will come through the interstate process, with the commission expected to discuss menhaden quotas for 2027 and 2028 during its october 2026 annual meeting. maine maine maine me maine coastal fisheries maine atlantic menhaden commercial fishing lobster fishery fishing quotas marine resources

nj-shbp-reform-working-group-2026-10-01.excerpt: The state, unions, health-care organizations and local-government representatives will study how to make coverage more affordable, but any changes will require further planning and approvals.
nj-shbp-reform-working-group-2026-10-01.text: new jersey opens health-benefits reform group as public-plan costs climb the state, unions, health-care organizations and local-government representatives will study how to make coverage more affordable, but any changes will require further planning and approvals. new jersey has formally launched a working group to rethink the state health benefits program, putting labor, state officials, health-care organizations and public-employer representatives in the same process as the state begins its october enrollment season. the group is expected to produce advisory recommendations for gov. mikie sherrill on how to slow cost growth while preserving coverage for public employees, retirees and participating employers, according to the governor’s oct. 1 announcement (office of the governor of new jersey: https://nj.gov/governor/news/2026/approved/20261001a.shtml). the launch fulfills a commitment in a sept. 2 agreement between the administration and 17 unions representing state employees. that agreement waived an increase in state workers’ health-benefit contribution rates for 2027 while giving labor a role in a broader review of the system. the state described the agreement as a response to structural cost pressures, not a final redesign of the plans. new jersey says its state, local-government and education health programs cover about 690,000 people combined (office of the governor of new jersey: https://nj.gov/governor/news/2026/approved/20260902b.shtml). the working group’s agenda reaches beyond the portion of premiums paid by employees. the governor’s office says members will examine how the state administers benefits, how insurers and providers are paid, the structure of provider networks, plan pricing, premium contributions, benefit design, participation rules, and the program’s governance and data systems. subcommittees will take up those subjects in more detail, and the administration says it may add outside experts and stakeholders as the review continues. that scope matters because new jersey’s public plans are not facing one uniform problem. state employees, local-government workers and school employees participate through programs with different plans, employers, governing bodies and legal requirements. independent reporting by the new jersey monitor found that a state commission approved an average 17.3% premium increase for local-government workers in september, while actuaries said the school employees’ plan needed an average 34.4% increase to fund claims, rebuild a month of surplus and repay a projected $90 million in state loans. the school-plan commission deadlocked, in part because one of its nine seats has been vacant (new jersey monitor: https://newjerseymonitor.com/2026/09/03/nj-panels-ok-rate-hike-for-public-worker-health-plans-deadlock-on-increase-for-teachers/). the dispute is therefore tied to more than household payroll deductions. higher premiums can affect municipal budgets, school districts and the state’s cost of employing and retaining workers. the new jersey monitor reported that state actuaries estimated the state workers’ plan would need to collect $397.2 million more in 2027 premiums than in 2026, although that figure includes increases that otherwise would have been paid by the state and employees. the state’s earlier budget materials also projected roughly $6.7 billion in fiscal 2026 health-benefit payments for active and retired enrollees for whom the state is responsible (new jersey treasury: https://nj.gov/treasury/omb/publications/26bib/bib.pdf). the timing puts members and employers in a transition period. the state health benefits program’s open-enrollment window for the 2026 plan year runs from oct. 1 through oct. 31, while the school employees’ health benefits program’s enrollment period is scheduled for oct. 26 through oct. 31, according to the state treasury’s benefits page (new jersey department of the treasury: https://www.nj.gov/treasury/pensions/documents/hb/oe2026/hb-sbc-state-active-26.shtml). the reform group’s recommendations will not change those windows or immediately alter anyone’s plan. the group’s first meeting is scheduled for oct. 16. the administration says it will continue detailed design and implementation planning in 2027, and any resulting changes could require collective bargaining, administrative action, procurement steps, commission votes, legislation or other legal approvals. that means the immediate result is a process and a set of questions, not a promised savings figure or a new benefit package. the central test will be whether the review produces changes that address provider and prescription-drug costs while giving workers, employers and taxpayers clearer information about how the system is financed. more misc misc. nj trenton trenton, new jersey new jersey health benefits public employees labor health care costs

ny-housing-counseling-hud-lawsuit-2026-0.excerpt: The lawsuit challenges the Trump administration’s decision not to award federally approved housing-counseling money, putting services used by thousands of New York households at risk.
ny-housing-counseling-hud-lawsuit-2026-0.text: new york sues hud over housing-counseling funds as $1m state award hangs in balance the lawsuit challenges the trump administration’s decision not to award federally approved housing-counseling money, putting services used by thousands of new york households at risk. new york attorney general letitia james sued the u.s. department of housing and urban development on wednesday, arguing that the agency unlawfully withheld federal housing-counseling money that supports homeowners, renters and prospective buyers across the state. the case was filed in the southern district of new york on the final day of the federal fiscal year, when the state said the underlying funds were scheduled to expire. the attorney general’s announcement is at https://ag.ny.gov/press-release/2026/attorney-general-james-sues-trump-administration-protect-housing-counseling-0. new york is seeking to protect roughly $1 million it applied for through the new york state housing finance agency. the money would be distributed among 22 hud-certified counseling organizations, with individual grants historically ranging from $20,000 to $100,000. the programs provide guidance on home purchases, rent and mortgage finances, foreclosure prevention, property maintenance and other housing decisions. the state’s complaint says new york has received this federal support regularly for about 13 years and submitted a complete application on may 22, but never received an award or explanation from hud. the lawsuit challenges a broader funding decision. the complaint says congress made approximately $57.5 million available for hud’s national housing counseling program, but hud had not obligated at least $56.1 million by the time the case was filed. new york argues that federal law requires hud to make assistance available to approved housing agencies and that congress did not authorize the department to eliminate or reduce the program on its own. those are allegations in the state’s complaint, not findings by the court. the filing is available at https://ag.ny.gov/sites/default/files/court-filings/state-of-new-york-v-u.s-department-of-housing-and-urban-development-complaint-2026.pdf. the immediate dispute grew out of a september 25 announcement by president donald trump seeking to cancel nearly $1 billion in federal spending through a so-called pocket rescission. the associated press reported that the package included hud housing-counseling money along with other programs the administration criticized as unnecessary or ideologically driven: https://apnews.com/article/46b356590699e6225f783c74e7ee3597. in its complaint, new york says the administration’s public criticism focused on the perceived views of some grant recipients rather than the housing services the program funds. hud and the administration could contest that characterization in court. the potential impact is more concrete than the statewide grant total. new york’s attorney general says the state’s 2024 funding helped counseling organizations serve more than 7,000 households with one-on-one assistance, provide nearly 2,800 households with financial help to improve living conditions, prevent more than 250 evictions and nearly 300 foreclosures, and help almost 300 first-time buyers close on homes. those figures describe the prior year’s reported results; they do not establish how many households would lose services immediately if the 2026 grant is not restored. housing counseling is designed to help people navigate decisions that can determine whether they remain housed or can buy a home. hud’s current new york resource page directs residents facing foreclosure or seeking homeownership information to hud-approved counselors and related assistance: https://www.hud.gov/states/new-york?custom2=0968e9f6-512c-4705-af0f-eb20f79a820f&og1=0968e9f6-512c-4705-af0f-eb20f79a820f. that background helps explain why the funding fight reaches beyond nonprofit budgets: counselors can work with borrowers and tenants before a missed payment, foreclosure filing or failed purchase becomes harder to resolve. james is asking the court to declare hud’s actions unlawful, require the department to maintain the program and preserve the unobligated money while the case proceeds. the complaint also asks the court to prevent the funds from being transferred, returned to the treasury or otherwise made unavailable in a way that would frustrate relief. the filing does not itself restore the grants. the next significant step is a court decision on whether to preserve the money and require hud to act; until then, new york’s 22 counseling organizations and the households they serve face uncertainty over the state’s expected federal support. new-york new-york new york ny new york new york state new york housing counseling hud housing affordability foreclosure prevention federal lawsuit

nyc-trick-or-streets-160-car-free-2026-0.excerpt: The citywide Halloween program will bring free activities, school events and neighborhood walking tours to Open Streets and plazas across all five boroughs.
nyc-trick-or-streets-160-car-free-2026-0.text: nyc plans record 160 car-free trick-or-streets locations for october the citywide halloween program will bring free activities, school events and neighborhood walking tours to open streets and plazas across all five boroughs. new york city is expanding its trick-or-streets program to a record 160 car-free open streets and plazas this october, giving families in all five boroughs a month of halloween and fall events instead of a single-night celebration. the city says the locations will host trick-or-treating, face painting, live entertainment and games. the new york city department of transportation also plans to distribute about 75,000 pieces of candy. abc7 new york reported the same announcement wednesday, sept. 30, and described the program as the city's largest trick-or-streets event to date: https://abc7ny.com/post/mayor-mamdani-announces-nycs-largest-trick-streets-new-york/19892758/ the effort is designed around temporary changes to public space. community organizations, schools and cultural groups will turn selected streets and plazas into pedestrian-oriented gathering places, while the municipal art society of new york will offer free guided walking tours focused on neighborhood history, architecture and public spaces. street lab is also partnering with nyc dot and city schools on halloween-themed play and creative activities at selected school sites. five signature events anchor the schedule. brooklyn's hillel plaza celebration is set for oct. 22 from 2 to 6 p.m.; staten island's water street open street follows oct. 24 from noon to 5 p.m.; and queens' austin street open street is scheduled for oct. 25 from 2 to 7 p.m. manhattan's canal street open street and division plaza event is planned for oct. 28 from 3 to 7 p.m., while the bronx's james baldwin plaza event is scheduled for halloween, oct. 31, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. the department of transportation's event page lists additional neighborhood programs beginning oct. 3, including activities on vanderbilt avenue in brooklyn and castleton avenue on staten island. the calendar includes block parties, parades, dog events and school-linked programming throughout the month. nyc dot says individual events can be delayed or canceled because of weather, so families should check the official calendar before traveling: https://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/html/pedestrians/trickorstreets.shtml the month-long format matters because the program is also a test of how new york uses streets beyond their usual transportation role. the city's announcement says the participating groups will use the spaces for community celebrations and, in some cases, to support local foot traffic and neighborhood businesses. the setup gives organizers control over their own programming while the city coordinates the street closures and works with partner agencies. mayor zohran kwame mamdani and nyc dot commissioner mike flynn announced the expansion on sept. 30. this is the fifth year of trick-or-streets, according to nyc dot, which says the initiative is meant to add pedestrian space during one of the busiest periods for new york streets. the full map and schedule remain the best guide to what is happening on a particular block, because the 160 locations will not all be active at the same time. the primary announcement is available from the nyc mayor's office: https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/09/mayor-mamdani-announces-largest-ever-trick-or-streets-with-160-c new-york new-york new york ny new york new york city, new york new york new york city halloween open streets nyc dot family events

ri-rural-health-cte-grants-2026-09-30.excerpt: Fourteen districts and schools will use Rural Health Transformation funds for healthcare training, from middle-school exploration to hands-on high school programs.
ri-rural-health-cte-grants-2026-09-30.text: rhode island directs $5.48m to rural school healthcare career pathways fourteen districts and schools will use rural health transformation funds for healthcare training, from middle-school exploration to hands-on high school programs. rhode island is directing more than $5.48 million in federal rural health transformation program awards to 14 school districts and schools, creating or expanding healthcare career pathways in rural communities across the state. the rhode island department of education announced the awards wednesday at ponaganset high school in glocester. the department said the grants are designed to connect students with health careers in stages: career awareness in kindergarten through fifth grade, exploration in grades six through eight, and preparation for work or further study in grades nine through twelve. the announcement was also reported independently by [providence business news](https://pbn.com/foster-glocester-lands-largest-share-of-5-48m-rural-healthcare-cte-grants/). the money comes through the federal rural health transformation program, which is supported by the centers for medicare and medicaid services and the u.s. department of health and human services. rhode island says the broader program is intended to improve access to coordinated healthcare in rural communities. ride said its awards will reach the state’s 18 rural communities, while helping schools build relationships with healthcare providers and colleges. foster-glocester regional school district received the largest award, $1,360,343. the district plans to anchor its pathway at ponaganset with an on-campus physical therapy clinic, physical and occupational therapy programs, and a middle-school wellness initiative that introduces younger students to health careers. that design gives students a local setting to encounter the field before they have to choose a high school concentration or postsecondary program. other awards target distinct parts of the healthcare pipeline. burrillville schools received $928,574 for a biomedical sciences pathway and a new ems and health sciences learning center, with possible training in emergency medical services, nursing, phlebotomy, physical therapy and related fields. east greenwich public schools received $710,619 to launch what ride described as rhode island’s first pre-medicine career and technical education program, while modernizing learning spaces and adding work-based learning, medical simulation and ai-supported clinical tools. westerly public schools received $658,773 to improve its medical careers and ems pathway with simulation equipment, virtual-reality training, staffing and professional development. smithfield received $513,690 to expand biomedical sciences and add behavioral-health training. scituate received $318,191 to extend its biomedical pathway through the k-12 grades and add sports medicine, community health and emergency-response options. the remaining grants range from $25,604 for jamestown’s lawn school to $268,454 for narragansett high school, with projects also planned in chariho, exeter-west greenwich, little compton, north kingstown, north smithfield and at the greene school. the awards are arriving as rhode island expands its overall career-and-technical-education system. ride reported that the number of high-quality cte programs statewide has grown from 203 in 2019 to 365, while participation has increased from about 12,000 students to more than 20,000. those figures are the department’s comparison, not an independent evaluation of the new grants, and the announcement does not provide a single completion date for the 14 projects. the next phase will be local implementation: districts will have to turn the awards into courses, equipment, work-based learning and partnerships that students can actually use. for rural rhode island, the practical test will be whether the new pathways make healthcare careers visible earlier, provide meaningful clinical or technical experience, and create durable connections between schools, employers and the communities that need healthcare workers. rhode-island rhode-island rhode island ri glocester rural rhode island rhode island career and technical education rural health transformation program healthcare workforce public schools education funding

vt-ag-timber-disaster-aid-2026-10-01.excerpt: Applications will open Oct. 26 for recovery payments tied to qualifying weather losses from 2023 and 2024, with first-phase awards covering up to 95% of eligible losses and capped at $75,000.
vt-ag-timber-disaster-aid-2026-10-01.text: vermont to open $31.7m disaster-aid program for farms and timber businesses applications will open oct. 26 for recovery payments tied to qualifying weather losses from 2023 and 2024, with first-phase awards covering up to 95% of eligible losses and capped at $75,000. vermont will begin accepting applications oct. 26 for a $31.7 million disaster-recovery program aimed at farms, forest landowners and logging contractors that suffered qualifying weather-related losses in 2023 or 2024. the state says the first phase will cover up to 95% of an applicant’s eligible losses, with a maximum payment of $75,000. [gov. phil scott’s office](https://governor.vermont.gov/press-release/governor-phil-scott-announces-317-million-vermont-agriculture-timber-disaster) announced the program sept. 30 with the vermont agency of agriculture, food & markets and the department of forests, parks and recreation. the program is built from federal block-grant funding authorized under the american relief act of 2025. vermont’s [legislative joint fiscal office](https://www.ljfo.vermont.gov/grants-reports/) separately lists a $31,771,557 usda farm service agency grant for compensation tied to crop, timber and livestock losses, including on-farm infrastructure and weather damage. the aid is designed for businesses that are still operating and can document both the loss and its connection to an eligible weather event. the state says applicants may seek reimbursement for damage that has already been repaired, rebuilt or replanted, or may commit to completing eligible restoration or replanting with the funds. the program is non-competitive: applicants who demonstrate eligible, otherwise-unmet losses are intended to receive a payment, subject to the program’s rules and available documentation. for agricultural producers, eligible categories may include damage to on-farm infrastructure, bare-ground practices needed after a weather event, future economic loss and market loss. for the forest economy, the program can cover standing-timber and harvested-timber losses, licensed-forester assessment costs, updates to forest stewardship plans and certain recovery costs for loggers reopening damaged harvest sites. those categories reflect the different ways floods, hard freezes, excessive moisture and other severe weather can disrupt a farm or a logging operation beyond the cost of one immediate repair. the program follows years of recovery pressure from vermont’s storms and floods. independent reporting by [vtdigger](https://vtdigger.org/2026/06/10/feds-approve-31-7-million-in-disaster-aid-for-flood-hit-vermont-farmers/) described the federal award as specialized relief for farmers with limited access to other federal disaster programs, including people facing infrastructure and market losses from the 2023 and 2024 events. the state’s current notice expands the practical reach to timber landowners and contracted loggers as well as agricultural producers. applicants should begin assembling ownership, lease or timber-sale records; parcel information; tax or business identification; descriptions of the damage; dated photographs; receipts, invoices, repair records or estimates; and records of other payments for the same loss. timber applicants may also need stand maps, forest-management information, timber-sale records, revenue documentation and a licensed forester assessment for some claims. the state says the online application window is expected to close dec. 31, with payments anticipated in early 2027. the first phase is not the entire program. vermont says a second phase will address larger infrastructure projects valued above $75,000 and up to $750,000 through a competitive grant process. receiving a phase-one payment will not by itself bar an applicant from phase two, but the second phase cannot pay for losses already covered by phase one or another funding source. the outstanding questions for producers are how many businesses will apply, how much documented loss the program will face and how quickly the state can turn the october filing window into payments. new-england new-england new england vt montpelier vermont vermont agriculture timber disaster assistance flood recovery weather losses farm economy

vt-williston-ice-protest-federal-charges.excerpt: Five people are accused of repeatedly blocking access to the Vermont facility, while separate state trespass cases are moving forward against protesters arrested this summer.
vt-williston-ice-protest-federal-charges.text: federal charges widen legal fight over williston ice facility protests five people are accused of repeatedly blocking access to the vermont facility, while separate state trespass cases are moving forward against protesters arrested this summer. federal prosecutors have charged five people accused of repeatedly blocking access to an immigration and customs enforcement facility in williston, opening a new legal track in a protest campaign that has already produced separate state trespass cases. the u.s. attorney’s office for the district of vermont said sept. 30 that peter booth, 58, of jericho; lexington kennedy, 22, of new york city; henry prensky, 80, of burlington; roan wade, 23, of red hook, new york; and sherri wormser, 57, of colchester were charged by information with obstructing access to the ice national criminal analysis and targeting center. the facility is in the white cap business park in williston, according to the [department of justice announcement](https://www.justice.gov/usao-vt/pr/five-people-charged-obstructing-access-federal-facility-williston-vermont). the allegations involve three protest dates. prosecutors say all five entered the building’s atrium on feb. 9 and used their bodies to block doors leading to the federal facility after warnings to disperse. the justice department says booth and prensky did so again on may 14, while kennedy and wade repeated the conduct on july 24. in each instance, the release says, access was restored after law enforcement removed protesters from the building. the federal case is narrower than a general challenge to protest activity: the charging document alleges obstruction of entrances and exits, not simply opposition to immigration policy. first assistant u.s. attorney jonathan ophardt said the blockades created safety risks for people working at the facility and required a substantial police response. those are the government’s allegations, not findings by a court. the defendants have not yet been scheduled for initial appearances. the justice department said each faces up to 30 days in prison and a fine of up to $5,000 if convicted, with any sentence to be set by the court under the applicable factors. the agency also said the five had not retained or been appointed counsel when the announcement was issued. all five are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. the charges add to a separate vermont prosecution arising from a july 24 demonstration at the same office complex. vermont attorney general charity clark filed unlawful-trespass cases against 13 people arrested during that sit-in; twelve pleaded not guilty at a sept. 24 arraignment, and the case of an 18-year-old was transferred to family court. [vermont public’s reporting](https://www.vermontpublic.org/local-news/2026-09-24/vermont-attorney-general-charges-protesters-for-trespassing-at-ice-surveillance-facility) said the state charge carries a maximum of three months in prison, a $500 fine, or both. vermont public reported oct. 1 that three of the five people named in the federal case also face state charges. the outlet described the federal action as an escalation after chittenden county state’s attorney sarah george previously declined to prosecute some protesters arrested during sit-ins, while clark’s office later took up the july cases. that split has made charging decisions part of the local debate over how vermont should respond to civil disobedience at the facility. for williston, the immediate issue is practical as well as legal. the white cap complex has become a recurring site of demonstrations, arrests and competing claims about public safety, federal immigration enforcement and protest rights. the next concrete step in the federal matter is the defendants’ initial court appearance; until then, the charging information establishes what prosecutors allege but does not resolve whether the conduct violated federal law or how the cases will affect future demonstrations. new-england new-england new england vt williston williston, vermont vermont williston immigration enforcement protests federal courts public safety
